fields.meta_title: Image Survey Builder With Picture Answers | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build an image survey from a prompt: picture answers, pick-one, pick-two or ranked votes, shuffled order, and every pick in a database you own.
fields.h1: Build an Image Survey With Pictures as the Answers
fields.hero_description: Build an image survey where people tap a picture to answer, and every pick lands in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Around Each Picture
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds the question, the image grid and the table that counts every pick, and a follow-up prompt changes any of them.
fields.feature_1:
Pictures as the answer options

Describe the question and the options, then add a photo for each one. Emergent builds a grid that people answer by tapping a picture, with a short label under every image.
fields.feature_2:
Pick one, pick two, or rank them

Set how people choose: a single favorite, a fixed number such as two of six, or a drag-to-rank order. A follow-up prompt switches the type without rebuilding the survey.
fields.feature_3:
A new image order for each person

The app can show the pictures in a fresh order to every respondent, so the top-left spot goes to a different design each time. Turn it off for any question that needs it.
fields.feature_4:
Every pick saved as a row you own

Each answer is a row in a database you own, with the image picked, the time and any tag you add, such as store or plan. Count the picks per image without exporting a file.
fields.feature_5:
One question per screen on a phone

Respondents see one question per screen, with the image grid fitted to a phone, and move on with a tap. Emergent puts no cap on responses, so it can go to your whole customer list.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain and an exportable codebase

Publish the survey on your own domain, which is included in Emergent and uses credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and reuse it for the next test.

fields.usecase_heading: How Four Teams Let the Picture Decide
fields.tab_content_1:
Tin B made it to print with 198 picks

Ashvale Tea Co. needed one tin design for its winter blend and had three. It showed 412 customers the three designs side by side, shuffled for each person, and asked which tin they would take off the shelf. Tin B drew 198 picks, tin A 121 and tin C 93. Tin B went to the printer.
fields.tab_content_2:
With 61 first-place votes, draft C won

Four logo drafts went to the 210 members of Duskwater Rowing Club, who dragged them into order from favorite to least. Of the 136 members who ranked them, 61 put draft C first and 31 put draft B first. The other two drafts got 22 each. The club board adopted draft C for next season's kit.
fields.tab_content_3:
Each customer picked two cakes from six

Hallowfen Bakery had room for two new cakes on its holiday menu and six candidates. It showed 288 customers a photo of each and asked them to pick two. The cranberry tart drew 141 picks and the pistachio roll 118, the top two of 576 picks. Both went on the December menu.
fields.tab_content_4:
Any hire under 10 correct photos retakes the quiz

Every new hire at Ketterly Hardware takes a 12-photo quiz: name the fastener in each picture. The pass mark is 10. This quarter, 14 of 18 new hires passed, and the store manager got the results in Slack. The 4 who scored under 10 retake it after a shift in the fastener aisle.

fields.howto_title: How to Run an Image Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to an image survey whose picks settle one decision, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Shoot every option the same way
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Give each image a short label
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Shuffle the order for each respondent
fields.howto_step_1_des: Name the one choice the picks will settle, such as which tin goes to the printer. Every image in the survey should be a real option for that choice. Put the decision in your prompt, and Emergent drafts the question around it.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Shoot each option at the same angle, against the same background and in the same light, then crop every photo to the same shape. If one photo is brighter or larger, you cannot tell whether people chose the design or the photo.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Under each picture, add two to four words that name it, like Tin B or Cranberry tart. The label names the option in your results table, and it lets people refer to a design when they explain their pick.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Pew Research Center notes that in self-administered surveys, people tend to choose items at the top of the list. Rotate the images so each one leads for some respondents, and keep a fixed order only where it means something, like small to large.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Choose how many each person picks
fields.howto_step_5_des: Ask for one pick when only one option can win, like a tin. Ask for two or three when several can, like menu spots. Use a ranking when you need the full order, and keep it to five images or fewer so the list fits one phone screen.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Ask one question about the reason
fields.howto_step_6_des: After the picture question, add one short open question: what made you pick it? The counts tell you which design won, and the comments tell you what to keep when you print it or redesign the others.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Test on a phone, then read the counts
fields.howto_step_7_des: Take the survey on your own phone before launch and check that every image loads sharp and every label fits. After launch, read each count against the number of people asked, not only against the other images.
fields.hero_prompt: Build an image survey that shows my 300 customers three new candle labels and saves each pick in a database.

faq_plan.a: An image survey is a survey whose answer options are pictures instead of words. Respondents tap the photo, design or logo they prefer, pick several, or rank a set into order. It fits choices people judge by eye, such as packaging, logos, menu items and room layouts.

faq_plan.q: How do I create an image survey?
faq_plan.a: Describe the question, the options and how many each person may pick in Emergent's AI survey builder, then add a photo for each option. Emergent builds the image grid, the answer rules and the table behind them. Take the survey on a phone yourself, change anything by prompt, and publish once every picture looks right.

faq_plan.q: How is an image quiz different from an image survey?
faq_plan.a: An image quiz has right answers: each picture question is marked correct or wrong, and the taker gets a score, often against a pass mark. An image survey has no right answer and counts preferences instead. Use a quiz to check what people know, like naming parts from photos, and a survey to choose between options.

faq_plan.q: What should a picture quiz maker let me control?
faq_plan.a: Scoring comes first: which picture is correct, the points per question and the pass mark. Then the ending, whether that is a score screen, a retake, or a result page with an email field that turns the quiz into a quiz funnel. You also want a text label on every photo.

faq_plan.q: How many pictures should one image survey question show?
faq_plan.a: Keep it to six or fewer for a single pick, laid out two across so a phone shows them with little scrolling. If you have more candidates, split them into two rounds and send the winners of each round to a final question.

faq_plan.q: How do I make an image survey work for screen reader users?
faq_plan.a: Give every image a text alternative that says what sets the option apart, such as "green tin, gold leaf pattern" rather than "option 2". WCAG 1.1.1 states that all non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose. Then try the survey with a screen reader before launch.

faq_plan.q: Can I run an image survey with my employees?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Picture questions suit staff decisions that come down to looks, such as a team shirt design, an office layout or a venue for the holiday party. Keep them separate from your employee engagement survey, which asks about the work itself, so a fun vote does not sit beside questions about managers.

faq_plan.q: How do I tell which picture won an image survey?
faq_plan.a: Compare each picture's picks with the number of people asked, not only with the other pictures. A lead of 150 picks to 140 out of 600 asked is close to a tie, and a second round settles it. In an app Emergent builds, every pick is a row in a database you own, so you can split the counts by store or plan.

faq_plan.q: Can an image survey show different pictures based on an earlier answer?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Ask a sorting question first, such as which store someone shops at, and show each group its own set of pictures. Emergent builds that branching from a prompt, and each answer keeps the group it came from, so one store's counts stay apart from another's.

faq_plan.q: Can an image survey end with a result instead of a vote count?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Give each picture points toward an outcome, then show the outcome with the most points on the last screen. A coffee quiz that shows six drinks and ends on a roast to try works this way. Emergent builds the scoring from a prompt, and each answer still lands in a database you own.

plan.angle: The top 10 is stock photo galleries plus survey-tool feature pages that show a picture question and stop there. This page shows four image surveys built from a prompt, each ending in a decision someone made from the picks: a packaging test, a ranked logo vote, a pick-two menu vote and a staff photo quiz with a pass mark. The how-to covers photographing options alike, labels, shuffled order and reading picks against the number asked.
